abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Purpose: this study aimed to investigate the potential of a novel 68Ga-labeled PSMA-targeted radiotracer, 68Ga-PSMA-33, as a diagnostic tool for prostate cancer in preclinical and pilot clinical studies. Methods: 68Ga-PSMA-33 was radiolabeled using an iQS-TS automated module, and its radiochemical purity and in vitro stability were analyzed via radio-HPLC. The specificity and binding affinity for PSMA were determined in LNCaP (PSMA+) cells. A head-to-head comparison with 68Ga-PSMA-617 was performed in murine models through biodistribution, pharmacokinetic, and micro-PET/CT imaging studies. The clinical phase involved 68Ga-PSMA-33 PET/CT imaging in seven patients with prostate cancer, two of whom also underwent 68Ga-PSMA-617 imaging for direct comparison. Semiquantitative assessment of physiologic biodistribution and tumor burden was conducted, and the radiation dosimetry of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was estimated. Results: 68Ga-PSMA-33 was efficiently prepared with a labeling yield of 77.5 ± 7.23%, radiochemical purity exceeding 99%, and specific activity of 45.28 ± 6.37 GBq/μmol. The labeled compound demonstrated a high affinity for PSMA (0.103 ± 0.03 nM), along with high hydrophilicity (Log P = −2.84 ± 0.13). Micro-PET/CT imaging revealed rapid clearance and prominent tumor uptake of the tracer, achieving a significantly higher tumor-to-muscle ratio than 68Ga-PSMA-617 (88.85 ± 8.39 vs 30.18 ± 3.39, p < 0.001) at 4 h postinjection. A total of nearly 400 tumor lesions were identified in PET/CT imaging across the 7 patients with prostate cancer. The mean SUVmax values of primary tumors, lymph node metastases, liver metastases, and bone metastases were 22.24 ± 4.77, 10.48 ± 2.16, 21.76 ± 3.82, and 30.25 ± 2.80 at 1 h postinjection, respectively. Clinical 68Ga-PSMA-33 PET/CT studies further confirmed its favorable biodistribution and kinetics, exhibiting a significantly higher tumor-to-muscle ratio than 68Ga-PSMA-617 at 3 h postinjection in both lymph node metastases (23.64 ± 6.68 vs 17.47 ± 7.53, p < 0.01) and bone metastases (83.33 ± 18.80 vs 61.63 ± 13.26, p < 0.001). The radiation dose of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was within an acceptable range, with an effective dose of (7.38 ± 1.44) × 10–3 mSv/MBq. The kidneys were the critical organ, receiving the highest absorbed dose of (7.35 ± 2.64) × 10–2 mGy/MBq. Conclusion: 68Ga-PSMA-33 demonstrated comparable tumor uptake while providing a higher tumor-to-background ratio and lower radiation exposure than 68Ga-PSMA-617, making it a promising novel tracer for prostate cancer diagnosis.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most common malignant neoplasm in men globally with a marked propensity for metastases and pronounced heterogeneity. The early detection and precise staging of PCa are crucial, as the patient survival rate declines sharply following metastasis. Additionally, personalized treatment strategies (surgery, radiation therapy, androgen deprivation therapy, chemotherapy, and immunotherapy) are tailored based on the accurate diagnosis and staging of PCa, thereby optimizing patient prognosis. , Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) screening is widely used for the initial diagnosis of PCa, but its accuracy is often challenged by a high rate of false-positive results and overdiagnosis. Therefore, multiple imaging modalities have been introduced for the detection of PCa, including transrectal ultrasound (TRUS), contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT), multiparametric magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), and positron emission tomography (PET). , PET/CT is of great value for the early diagnosis and staging of malignant tumors. PET/CT combined with a specific radiotracer further contributes to the molecular phenotyping, which will tailor the targeted treatment. Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA), a transmembrane glutamate carboxypeptidase markedly overexpressed on PCa cells, is consequently recognized as an independent biomarker of poor prognosis. Most metastatic lesions in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) patients exhibit PSMA positivity, and notably, PSMA overexpression is independently associated with diminished overall survival.

In recent years, PSMA-targeted theragnostics has revolutionized the management of PCa. A large number of PSMA-targeting radiopharmaceuticals labeled with radionuclides such as 18F, 68Ga, 64Cu, 177Lu, 161Tb, 211At, 212Pb, and 225Ac have been developed and evaluated in this field. Among them, FDA-approved 68Ga-PSMA-11, 18F-DCFPyL, and 18F-rhPSMA-7.3 were used for staging and restaging of PCa as well as assessing therapeutic efficacy. , Although widely utilized in clinical study, 68Ga-PSMA-617 has not yet been officially approved. However, good efficacy results were reported for radionuclide therapy using 177Lu-PSMA-617, which was accordingly recommended in the latest NCCN guidelines. The emergence of α-emitters such as 225Ac has further improved the efficacy of PSMA-RLT, with 225Ac-PSMA-617 proving beneficial for patients with advanced mCRPC refractory to or progressing after 177Lu-PSMA-617 therapy. However, dose escalation of these agents is limited by dose-dependent toxicity in critical organs (kidneys, bone marrow, and salivary glands). Especially for 225Ac-PSMA-617, as its higher radiation energy increases the radiation burden on kidneys and salivary glands, leading to higher rates of renal impairment and xerostomia. Thus, there is a high clinical demand for further improving the pharmacokinetic profile of PSMA-617 to minimize its side effects.

Hereby, a novel PSMA-targeted radiotracer, 68Ga-PSMA-33 (Figure S1), was developed by introducing dual cyclic motifs and heteroatoms into the linker region of PSMA-617 to fine-tune the physicochemical and pharmacokinetic properties. The potential of 68Ga-PSMA-33 as an alternative PET imaging radiotracer for PCa detection was assessed via a head-to-head comparison with 68Ga-PSMA-617 in both preclinical and pilot clinical investigations.

sec.title: Materials
sec.p: PSMA-33 and PSMA-617 were synthesized by Tianjin Hengrui Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd. The chemical purity of both compounds was determined to be greater than 95%. Hydrochloric acid and ultrapure water were obtained from Merck (Germany). 2-(phosphonomethyl)-pentanedioic acid (2-PMPA) and sodium acetate were purchased from Macklin (China). 0.9% sodium chloride injection was provided by Otsuka (China). Other commercially available chemical reagents are of analytical grade and can be used directly without further purification. A Ge-68/Ga-68 generator was used with an iQS-theranostics synthesizer (iQS-TS, ITG GmbH, Germany) for automated radiolabeling. Radiochemical purity was analyzed by radio-HPLC (B-FC-1000F, Bioscan, USA) equipped with a Waters Xbridge C18 column (5 μm, 250 × 10 mm, Milford, USA) and radio-TLC (Scan-RAM, Sheffield, UK). Radioactivity was measured using a γ-counter (Wizard 2, PerkinElmer, USA). Inveon micro-PET/CT (Siemens Medical Solutions, Germany) and uMI 780 PET/CT scanner (United Imaging Healthcare, China) were used for in vivo imaging.

sec.title: Tumor Cell Line and Mouse Model
sec.p: The Human prostate adenocarcinoma LNCaP cell line was procured from the Cell Bank of Shanghai Institutes for Biological Sciences. Cells were cultured in RPMI-1640 medium supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (Gibco, USA) and 1% penicillin–streptomycin (100 U/mL; Beyotime, China) and maintained at 37 °C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO2 until use during the logarithmic growth phase. Healthy male ICR mice (4–6 weeks, 20 – 25g) and BALB/c nude mice (4–6 weeks, 18 – 25g) were purchased from BioHermes Biomedical Science and Technology Co., Ltd. (China). LNCaP xenograft models were established in BALB/c nude mice by the subcutaneous inoculation of 1 × 107 cells into the right armpit for subsequent micro-PET/CT imaging and biodistribution studies once the tumor volume reached 200 mm3. The protocol for all animal procedures was approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of Nanjing First Hospital (Approval No. DWSY-2000124).

sec.title: Radiolabeling PSMA-33/PSMA-617 with 68Ga and Quality Control
sec.p: Radiolabeling was performed using an iQS-TS automated module. Briefly, 68Ga was eluted from Ge-68/Ga-68 generator using 0.05 M HCl (4.0 mL) and reacted with the precursor (20 μg PSMA-33 or PSMA-617) in sodium acetate buffer (1.0 mL, pH 8.0) at 95 °C for 14 min. The mixture was then purified via a Sep-Pak C18 cartridge, and the final product was formulated in saline/medium after ethanol elution. Radiopharmaceutical quality control was subsequently performed, and the product was visually inspected for appearance. The radiochemical purity of the saline-formulated sample was determined by radio-HPLC with a gradient of water/acetonitrile (both containing 0.1% trifluoroacetic acid (TFA)) at a 1.0 mL/min flow rate. The linear gradient started from 95%–90% A (0.1% TFA in water) and 5%–10% B (0.1% TFA in acetonitrile) for 5 min and then changed linearly to 90%–20% A and 10%–80% B for 15 min. Finally, the mobile phase returned linearly to 100% B at the run end. The purity of PSMA-33 was detected by HPLC using the same linear gradient, with UV detection at 220 nm. Radio-TLC analysis was performed on ITLC-SG paper (Agilent, US) with a 0.1 M ammonium acetate/methanol (1:1, v/v) as the developing solvent. Specific activity and ethanol content were calculated, and pH was measured using indicator paper.

sec.title: Lipophilicity and Stability Study
sec.p: The lipophilicity of 68Ga-PSMA-33 and 68Ga-PSMA-617 was determined using the shake-flask method by partitioning between n-octanol and PBS (pH 7.4). The log P values, calculated from three independent experiments, are reported as mean ± SD. Meanwhile, the in vitro stability of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was assessed by incubating in PBS or fresh human serum at 37 °C, with radiochemical purity analyzed by radio-HPLC at 1, 2, and 4 h.

sec.title: Cell Uptake and Binding Affinity
sec.p: LNCaP cells were plated in 24-well plates at a density of 1 × 105 cells per well and cultured overnight. For the uptake and blocking experiments, cells were incubated with 68Ga-PSMA-33 or 68Ga-PSMA-617 (37 kBq/well in 500 μL) at 37 °C for 0.5, 1, 2, and 4 h, respectively. The blocking group cells were saturated with excess 2-PMPA (1 μM, 500 μL) before adding 68Ga-PSMA-33 (37 kBq, 500 μL). For the competitive binding assay, cells were coincubated with 68Ga-PSMA-33 or 68Ga-PSMA-617 (37 kBq, 500 μL) and increasing concentrations of 2-PMPA (10–8 – 102 μM, 500 μL) for 1 h at 37 °C. Cell-bound radioactivity was then measured by a γ-counter for the calculation of half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50).

sec.title: Pharmacokinetic Analysis and Ex-Vivo Biodistribution
sec.p: 68Ga-PSMA-33 or 68Ga-PSMA-617 (7.4 MBq) was injected into normal ICR male mice (2 groups, n = 4/group) via the tail vein. The blood samples were collected from the tail at 2, 5, 10, 15, 30, 60, and 120 min post-injection and weighed. Radioactivity was measured using a γ-counter, and time–activity curves were plotted to derive pharmacokinetic parameters. For biodistribution, LNCaP xenograft tumor-bearing mice (n = 4/group) were injected with 68Ga-PSMA-33 (7.4 MBq) and sacrificed at different time points (5, 30, 60, 120, and 240 min). The blocking group mice were preinjected with excess 2-PMPA (20 mg/kg) via the tail vein 30 min prior to tracer administration. Blood, tumors, and major organs were harvested, weighed, and measured by a γ-counter; the results were expressed as a percentage of injected dose per gram of tissue (%ID/g).

sec.title: Micro-PET/CT Imaging
sec.p: LNCaP-xenografted mice were anesthetized with isoflurane (RWD, China) and underwent micro-PET/CT scans at 0.5, 1, 2, and 4 h after intravenous injection of 68Ga-PSMA-33 (7.4 MBq). A blocking group was preadministered 2-PMPA (20 mg/kg) 30 min prior to the tracer. For comparison, a separate group of mice (n = 3) was injected with 68Ga-PSMA-617 and scanned using the same protocol. A low-dose CT scan (80 kV, 500 μA, 328 s scan time, 110.3 μm pixel size) was first acquired for anatomical reference and attenuation correction, followed immediately by a 10 min static PET acquisition (128 × 128 × 159 matrix, 350–650 keV). Images were reconstructed with three-dimensional ordered-subset expectation maximum algorithm (3D-OSEM) and analyzed using Inevon Research Workplace 4.1 software. The concentration of radioactivity accumulated in the tumor and major organs was quantified by manually delineating the region of interest (ROI), with results expressed as %ID/g.

sec.title: Preliminary Clinical PET/CT Imaging in Humans
sec.p: A total of seven patients were enrolled in this clinical study, and all provided written informed consent. The study protocol received approval from the Ethics Committee of Nanjing First Hospital (KY20220825-05) and was registered on ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06054789). All patients received an intravenous injection of 68Ga-PSMA-33 (207.99 ± 43.64 MBq) and underwent PET/CT scans on a uMI 780 scanner at 0.5, 1, 2, and 3 h postinjection (p.i.). For comparison, two of these patients were additionally injected with 68Ga-PSMA-617 (172.37 ± 6.36 MBq) on the preceding day and scanned at 2 and 3 h p.i. A nonenhanced CT scan (120 kV, mA modulation, pitch 0.988, slice thickness 3.0 mm, increment 1.5 mm) was obtained, followed by a whole-body PET acquisition (3 min/bed, field of view 60 cm, 256 × 256 matrix) from the vertex to proximal legs. PET images were reconstructed using an ordered subset expectation maximization algorithm with 4 iterations/8 subsets and Gaussian filtering to an in-plane spatial resolution of 3 mm at full-width at half-maximum. PET/CT fusion and ROI delineation were then performed on a uMI 780 workstation for data analysis. Lesions with uptake exceeding background or blood pool were defined as PSMA-positive for semiquantitative analysis using SUVmax. For patients with multiple lesions, the one with the highest SUVmax was designated as the index tumor, and all lesions were analyzed when five or fewer were present; otherwise, five measurable lesions were randomly selected for analysis. The lesion was eventually confirmed as PCa by pathology, and PSMA expression was evaluated by immunohistochemistry.

sec.title: Assessment of Safety and Tolerability
sec.p: All clinically significant abnormal findings (subjective or physician’s observed) occurring from the administration of 68Ga-PSMA-33 to the end of the clinical trial (3 h after 68Ga-PSMA-33 injection) were recorded and defined as adverse events. The signs, symptoms, or illnesses that occurred before the administration of 68Ga-PSMA-33 were considered adverse events only if they were exacerbated. Vital signs (ECG, blood pressure, heart rate, respiratory rate, and body temperature) were monitored before, immediately after, and 3 h after 68Ga-PSMA-33 injection.

sec.title: Radiation Dosimetry
sec.p: Organ radiation dosimetry for 68Ga-PSMA-33 was estimated by using accumulated radioactivity in four sequential PET images. The results were further analyzed with OLINDA/EXM version 2.1 software (Hermes Medical Solutions AB) to calculate the organ absorbed doses and the effective dose.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Quantitative data were described as mean ± SD, and data normality was evaluated using the Shapiro–Wilk test. Differences between independent groups were analyzed by Student’s t-test, with p < 0.05 defining statistical significance. Analyses were conducted using SPSS 22.0 and GraphPad Prism 9.0 software.

sec.title: Radiolabeling and Quality Control of 68Ga-PSMA-33 and 68Ga-PSMA-617
sec.p: 68Ga-PSMA-33 and 68Ga-PSMA-617 were successfully radiolabeled within 14 min, with yield rates of 77.5 ± 7.23% and 80.1 ± 6.55%, respectively. The molar activity of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was determined to be 45.28 ± 6.37 GBq/μmol. Purity analysis of the compound is shown in Figure S2. Radio-HPLC confirmed high radiochemical purity (>99%) for 68Ga-PSMA-33 and 68Ga-PSMA-617, with retention times of 13.02 ± 0.04 min and 13.15 ± 0.01 min, respectively. As summarized in Table , the final injection formulations of both radiotracers met all quality control requirements.

sec.title: Partition Coefficient and Stability
sec.p: The lipophilicity of radiotracers was determined by the partition coefficient Log P. The Log P of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was −2.84 ± 0.13, slightly lower than that of 68Ga-PSMA-617 (−2.71 ± 0.12), indicating a higher hydrophilic, but there is no significant difference statistically (p > 0.05). In vitro stability of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was evaluated using radio-HPLC. The radiochemical purity of 68Ga-PSMA-33 remained ≥99% after incubation in PBS and human serum at 37 °C for 4 h (Figure S3). The result indicated that 68Ga-PSMA-33 was sufficiently stable for further study.

sec.title: In Vitro Cell Binding Affinity and Uptake
sec.p: Competitive cell binding assays revealed that 2-PMPA inhibited the binding of 68Ga-PSMA-33 to LNCaP cells in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure A). The IC50 value of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was 0.103 ± 0.03 nM, which was at the same order of magnitude as that of 68Ga-PSMA-617 (0.125 ± 0.03 nM). Cell uptake and blocking studies were conducted to evaluate the specificity of 68Ga-PSMA-33 in vitro (Figure B). The uptake of 68Ga-PSMA-33 in LNCaP cells increased over time: from an initial value of 5.47 ± 0.61 IA %/106 at 0.5 h to 10.80 ± 0.49 IA %/106 at 4 h, and this uptake was significantly blocked by coincubation with 2-PMPA for 4 h, resulting in a final value of 1.37 ± 0.11 IA %/106 (−87.33%). In comparison, the uptake of 68Ga-PSMA-617 in LNCaP cells was 11.07 ± 0.63 IA %/106 at 4 h, there were no statistically significant differences between them (p > 0.05).

caption.p: (A) Competitive binding curves for IC50 determination of 68Ga-PSMA-33 and 68Ga-PSMA-617 in LNCaP cells, using 2-PMPA as a competitive inhibitor. (B) Cell uptake of 68Ga-PSMA-33 and 68Ga-PSMA-617 in LNCaP cells at different time points.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics in Blood and Biodistribution
sec.p: Blood pharmacokinetics in normal ICR mice revealed rapid distribution and elimination for both 68Ga-PSMA-33 and 68Ga-PSMA-617. The elimination half-life of 68Ga-PSMA-33 (7.65 ± 0.09 min) was shorter than 68Ga-PSMA-617 (13.10 ± 0.05 min) (Figure S4). Biodistribution studies in LNCaP tumor-bearing models further characterized the metabolic profile and targeting specificity of 68Ga-PSMA-33 (Table S1). Tumor uptake peaked at 60 min p.i. (10.88 ± 0.57%ID/g) and was markedly blocked by 2-PMPA (2.41 ± 0.40% ID/g, p < 0.0001, t = 24.43), confirming PSMA-mediated specificity. The tracer was rapidly cleared from blood and nontarget organs, resulting in high tumor-to-liver (16.57 ± 3.09) and tumor-to-muscle (89.40 ± 9.76) ratios at 240 min. Observed kidney uptake (16.91 ± 0.91, 10.63 ± 1.27, and 5.61 ± 0.85%ID/g at 30, 60, and 120 min, respectively) supported renal clearance as the primary elimination route. Notably, the high accumulation of 68Ga-PSMA-33 in kidneys could also be blocked by 2-PMPA (3.65 ± 0.61% ID/g, p < 0.0001, t = 9.914) at 60 min p.i.

sec.title: Micro-PET/CT Imaging
sec.p: The maximum intensity projection (MIP) images of 68Ga-PSMA-33 and 68Ga-PSMA-617 in LNCaP-xenograft tumor-bearing mice at 0.5, 1, 2, and 4h p.i. are shown in Figure . LNCaP-xenograft tumors were clearly visible as early as 0.5 h p.i., with a tumor uptake value of 10.60 ± 0.75%ID/g. The tumor-to-muscle ratio (18.59 ± 2.83) and tumor uptake (10.97 ± 1.03%ID/g) at 1 h p.i. were significantly higher than those in the blocking group (2.17 ± 0.68%ID/g, p < 0.001, t = 12.75), demonstrating the specificity of 68Ga-PSMA-33 for PSMA-positive tumors. As a control, 68Ga-PSMA-617 micro-PET/CT was performed and displayed comparable tumor uptake (11.87 ± 1.82%ID/g) and an early tumor-to-muscle ratio (18.16 ± 3.48 at 1 h p.i.). While the tumor uptake values between the two tracers were not significantly different (p > 0.05), 68Ga-PSMA-33 exhibited a higher tumor-to-muscle ratio (88.85 ± 8.39 vs 30.18 ± 3.39 for 68Ga-PSMA-617, p < 0.001, t = 12.23) at 4 h p.i., indicating superior imaging contrast over time. In addition, both tracers showed prominent radioactivity in the kidneys and bladder, consistent with renal clearance, with minimal background signal in other normal tissues. Notably, the renal uptake of 68Ga-PSMA-33 (5.97 ± 0.97%ID/g) was significantly lower than that of 68Ga-PSMA-617 (10.13 ± 2.22%ID/g, p < 0.05, t = 2.98) at 2 h p.i., which could also be obviously reduced by 2-PMPA.

caption.p: (A) Micro-PET/CT images of LNCaP tumor-bearing mice at different time points after injection of 68Ga-PSMA-33. (B) Micro-PET/CT images of LNCaP tumor-bearing mice at different time points after injection of 68Ga-PSMA-617. (C) Blocked by excess 2-PMPA before injection of 68Ga-PSMA-33, the blocking ratio [(total radioactivity uptakeblocked radioactivity uptake)/total radioactivity uptake] was 79.81 ± 7.50% at 1 h. (D) Uptake (%ID/g) of tumor and tumor/muscle.

sec.title: 68Ga-PSMA-33 PET/CT Imaging in Prostate Cancer Patients
sec.p: The clinical characteristics and the lesions detected by PSMA PET/CT were shown in Table . All patients tolerated 68Ga-PSMA-33 well, with no observed adverse events. Detailed safety and tolerance evaluations are presented in Table S2. As shown in Figure and >Table S3, 68Ga-PSMA-33 showed intensive uptake in the lacrimal gland, parotid gland, submandibular gland, duodenum, and kidney, with the SUVmax values of 8.12 ± 2.39, 10.01 ± 1.51, 13.49 ± 5.35, 9.37 ± 0.53, and 25.06 ± 8.25 at 1 h p.i., respectively. The uptake in the lacrimal glands (12.33 ± 0.75), parotid gland (13.73 ± 1.27), submandibular gland (17.26 ± 9.05), duodenum (12.69 ± 0.91), and kidney (27.65 ± 11.12) continued to increase at 3 h p.i. Other organs such as heart, brain, lung, bone, muscle, and so on showed relatively low uptake and did not change significantly between 1 and 3 h p.i. PSMA PET/CT imaging revealed positive lesions in the prostate and multiple metastatic lesions for all seven patients (Figure S5). In brief, nearly 400 lesions were detected, including 7 primary PCa lesions, 37 lymph node metastases (LN metastases), 23 liver metastases, and over 300 bone metastases. The average SUVmax values of primary PCa lesions, LN metastases, liver metastases, and bone metastases were 22.24 ± 4.77, 10.48 ± 2.16, 21.76 ± 3.82, and 30.25 ± 2.80 at 1 h p.i., respectively. These values significantly increased at 3 h p.i. with average SUVmax values of 33.96 ± 3.04, 15.44 ± 3.30, 28.10 ± 5.29, and 40.25 ± 2.65, respectively. Accordingly, the low uptake in background (muscle: with average SUVmax values of 0.73 ± 0.20 at 1 h p.i. and 0.61 ± 0.22 at 3 h p.i.) and high accumulation in lesions contributed to the high ratio of primary tumor-to-muscle (29.23 ± 8.30 at 1 h p.i. and 47.52 ± 8.83 at 3 h p.i.), LN metastases-to-muscle (16.27 ± 4.55 at 1 h p.i. and 27.90 ± 6.34 at 3 h p.i.), liver metastases-to-muscle (42.66 ± 7.48 at 1 h p.i. and 49.30 ± 9.28 at 3 h p.i.), and bone metastases-to-muscle (50.72 ± 9.75 at 1 h p.i. and 80.83 ± 10.62 at 3 h p.i.), which provided a high image contrast.

sec.title: PET Imaging Comparison between 68Ga-PSMA-33 and 68Ga-PSMA-617
sec.p: Two patients underwent both 68Ga-PSMA-33 and 68Ga-PSMA-617 injections for direct comparison. All PSMA lesions detected by 68Ga-PSMA-617 were also found by 68Ga-PSMA-33. The detailed data of the comparison are shown in Table S4. From the comparison, the local tumor uptake of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was slightly higher than that of 68Ga-PSMA-617, while the uptake in lymph nodes and bone metastases was similar. As shown in Figure , both 68Ga-PSMA-33 and 68Ga-PSMA-617 displayed a similar distribution in normal organs. The uptake of 68Ga-PSMA-33 in most organs, such as the brain, heart, lung, stomach, pancreas, bone, muscle, liver, spleen, submandibular gland, sublingual gland, and duodenum was lower than that of 68Ga-PSMA-617, but the differences were not statistically significant. Additionally, similar to the results of previous animal studies, 68Ga-PSMA-33 was prone to excretion via the kidney and showed a significantly higher tumor-to-muscle ratio than that of 68Ga-PSMA-617 (LN metastases: 23.64 ± 6.68 vs 17.47 ± 7.53, p < 0.01, t = 5.53; bone metastases: 83.33 ± 18.80 vs 61.63 ± 13.26, p < 0.001, t = 7.27) at 3 h p.i.

(A) MIP image injected with 68Ga-PSMA-33. (B) MIP image injected with 68Ga-PSMA-617. (C, E) Fused axial PET/CT image of the patient injected with 68Ga-PSMA-33. (D, F) Fused axial PET/CT image of the patient injected with 68Ga-PSMA-617. The blue arrow indicated the LN metastasis, and the green arrow indicated the bone metastasis.

sec.title: Estimation of Radiation Dosimetry in Humans
sec.p: The estimated radiation-absorbed dose for different organs is presented in Table , most organs received low radiation exposure. The kidneys were identified as the critical organ, receiving the highest absorbed dose of (7.35 ± 2.64) × 10–2 mGy/MBq, followed by the adrenals (1.51 ± 0.317) × 10–2 mGy/MBq) and liver ((1.15 ± 0.439) × 10–2 mGy/MBq). Additionally, the radiation-absorbed dose for salivary glands was (9.22 ± 4.30) × 10–3 mGy/MBq. The average effective dose of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was (7.38 ± 1.44) × 10–3 mSv/MBq.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: PSMA is a pivotal and well-established molecular target in PCa, and its distinct properties have underpinned the development of new diagnostic and therapeutic strategies. Numerous studies have demonstrated the high sensitivity and specificity of PSMA-targeted imaging and the superior detection rates achieved with a growing array of novel PSMA-targeted radiopharmaceuticals. In particular, PSMA PET imaging can guide PSMA-targeted radionuclide therapy, thereby contributing to improved outcomes in advanced or high-risk PCa. Herein, a novel PSMA precursor (PSMA-33) was synthesized by modifying the structure of PSMA-617 to improve tumor accumulation while accelerating clearance from nontarget organs. In view of the merits of the 68Ga/177Lu partner in the integrated radionuclide theragnositics, we first labeled PSMA-33 with 68Ga and verified its potentiality for PCa imaging in the preclinical study and validated its clinical application.

68Ga-PSMA-33 was automatically radiosynthesized with a sufficiently high radiochemical yield (70 – 85%) and a favorable specific activity (consistently >40 GBq/μmol) to meet the demand for the imaging needs of at least 5 patients from a single synthesis. Additionally, 68Ga-PSMA-33 exhibited a lower Log P value and a shorter elimination half-life than 68Ga-PSMA-617 (−2.84 ± 0.13 vs – 2.71 ± 0.12, 7.65 ± 0.09 vs 13.10 ± 0.05 min, respectively), indicating the significant improvement of the hydrophilicity and clearance rate following structural optimization as expected.

The tumor-targeting affinity of 68Ga-PSMA-33 for PSMA was evaluated using PSMA-positive LNCaP cells and xenograft tumor models. Generally, the accumulation of 68Ga-PSMA-33 in LNCaP cells and xenograft tumors was comparable to that of 68Ga-PSMA-617. The uptake was substantially blocked by the PSMA inhibitor 2-PMPA, confirming that the high uptake of 68Ga-PSMA-33 is specifically mediated by PSMA. The high affinity of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was demonstrated by an IC50 value of 0.103 ± 0.03 nM in LNCaP cells, which was slightly lower than that of 68Ga-PSMA-617 (0.125 ± 0.03 nM).

The ex vivo biodistribution study demonstrated that 68Ga-PSMA-33 was rapidly cleared from major organs and exhibited low background uptake with predominant accumulation observed in the kidneys and bladder. Furthermore, 68Ga-PSMA-33 uptake in the kidneys was significantly reduced by the coinjection with 2-PMPA, revealing that its high renal uptake is due not only to excretion via the urinary tract but also to physiological PSMA expression in the kidneys.

Micro-PET/CT imaging in tumor-bearing mice noninvasively confirmed the biodistribution profile observed in the ex vivo studies. The LNCaP tumors were clearly visualized at 1 h after the injection of 68Ga-PSMA-33, with the %ID/g of 10.97 ± 1.03, which was comparable to that of 68Ga-PSMA-617 (11.87 ± 1.82%ID/g). But it is noteworthy that 68Ga-PSMA-33 achieved a significantly higher tumor-to-muscle ratio than 68Ga-PSMA-617 (88.85 ± 8.39 vs 30.18 ± 3.39 at 4 h p.i.). This superior contrast is attributed to its sufficient tumor uptake, enhanced hydrophilicity, and rapid systemic clearance. Meanwhile, the lower renal uptake of 68Ga-PSMA-33 compared to 68Ga-PSMA-617 demonstrates that the structural modification of the linker region has effectively improved the pharmacokinetic properties of the compound. In addition, the absence of detectable bone uptake in the micro-PET/CT images suggests high in vivo stability of 68Ga-PSMA-33, with no significant dissociation of the 68Ga radionuclide.

On the basis of the favorable preclinical results and with the approval of the Ethics Committee of Nanjing First Hospital, a subsequent first-in-human study of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was initiated. We enrolled seven PCa patients in this prospective study for 68Ga-PSMA-33 PET/CT imaging. In terms of its biodistribution profile, 68Ga-PSMA-33 primarily accumulated in PSMA-expressing organs (lacrimal and salivary glands) or lesions and was cleared via the urinary system (kidneys and bladder). This biodistribution pattern is consistent with that of other well-documented Glu-urea-based PSMA probes. Additionally, we found that the overall biodistribution of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was similar between humans and mice, but the negligible salivary gland uptake in mice does not accurately predict the significant uptake observed in patients. This indicates that the murine model has a limited predictive value for tracer distribution in human salivary glands. The underlying species variation in PSMA expression patterns likely explains this observed difference.

The clinical PET/CT study confirmed the high diagnostic performance of 68Ga-PSMA-33 for the accurate localization of primary and metastatic PCa lesions. Among the seven recruited PCa patients, nearly 400 tumor sites were detected, and over 80% of these lesions exhibited increasing SUVmax values from 0.5 to 3 h p.i. Nontarget organs (excluding those with physiological PSMA expression) showed low and stable uptake between 1 and 3 h p.i. This suggests that imaging within this time window may be suitable, although the optimal timing should be confirmed in future studies with larger cohorts. There were no significant differences between 68Ga-PSMA-33 and 68Ga-PSMA-617 in the number of identified PCa lesions or the qualitative visual assessment scores. Notably, the tumor-to-muscle ratio of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was significantly higher than that of 68Ga-PSMA-617 at 3h p.i. (primary: 12.01 ± 4.96 vs 7.42 ± 1.14, LN metastases: 23.64 ± 6.68 vs 17.47 ± 7.53 and bone metastases: 83.33 ± 18.80 vs 61.63 ± 13.26, respectively). Through structural modifications, not only was the expected accelerated muscle clearance achieved, but the local tumor uptake of 68Ga-PSMA-33 also exhibited a modest improvement. The specific accumulation of 68Ga-PSMA-33 in PCa lesions and rapid clearance from nontarget organs facilitates sufficient tumor contrast images and low toxicity. In addition, 68Ga-PSMA-33 (SUVmax = 25.06 ± 8.25) demonstrated lower renal uptake compared to the clinically approved diagnostic agent 68Ga-PSMA-11 (SUVmax = 37.72 ± 22.1), which was accompanied by improved safety and diagnostic efficacy.

Internal radiation dosimetry estimates from 5 patients indicated that the absorbed doses for all organs were well within acceptable limits. The kidneys were the dose-limiting organ, receiving an absorbed dose of (7.35 ± 2.64) × 10–2 mGy/MBq. This value is considerably lower than the renal doses reported for other Glu-urea-based PSMA probes, such as 68Ga-PSMA-11 (0.262 mGy/MBq), 68Ga-PSMA-617 (0.206 mGy/MBq), 18F-PSMA-1007 (0.17 mGy/MBq), and 18F-DCFPyL (0.0945 mGy/MBq). −
The average effective dose of 68Ga-PSMA-33 was calculated to be (7.38 ± 1.44) × 10–3 mSv/MBq, which is comparable to established clinical standards and is significantly lower than that of 68Ga-PSMA-617 (0.021 mSv/MBq) as well as 68Ga-PSMA-11 (0.0167 mSv/MBq). , Additionally, the PSMA-33 ligand can be utilized for PCa therapy by simply substituting 68Ga with 177Lu. Its high hydrophilicity and rapid clearance are anticipated to reduce renal radiation exposure, thereby improving the therapeutic index and potentially enhancing treatment outcomes.

However, the limited sample size of this initial study may restrict the generalizability of the diagnostic efficacy findings. This preliminary study was designed to evaluate the preclinical profile and the initial clinical diagnostic potential of the probe. Consequently, a limited number of PCa patients without stratification by prior treatment history were included. Generally, the linker modification improved the pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of 68Ga-PSMA-33, leading to a significant reduction in radiation exposure to nontarget organs, particularly the kidneys. However, no marked improvement was observed in the radioactive uptake of salivary glands, indicating that 68Ga-PSMA-33 still cannot circumvent the issue of physiological uptake inherent to PSMA-targeted tracers. Furthermore, the pilot clinical study confirmed that 68Ga-PSMA-33 PET/CT provided excellent quality images with high SUV values and superior tumor-to-muscle ratios, suggesting potential for enhanced diagnostic efficacy. Nevertheless, constrained by the short half-life of 68Ga, imaging was performed only up to 4 h. The SUVmax in tumor lesions kept increasing without reaching the peak, especially for lymph node and bone metastases. Future studies extending the imaging time or employing radionuclides with longer half-lives could determine the optimal time window for peak tumor uptake. Multiple large-scale head-to-head comparison studies of 68Ga-PSMA-33 with 68Ga-PSMA-617 and a therapeutic study of 177Lu-PSMA-33 are ongoing.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: Preclinical and first-in-human studies confirmed that 68Ga-PSMA-33 highly and selectively accumulated in prostate tumors, demonstrating an imaging performance visually equivalent to that of 68Ga-PSMA-617. The favorable uptake and retention in both primary and metastatic PCa lesions, high tumor-to-background ratios, and reasonably low radiation exposure highlight the potential of 68Ga-PSMA-33 for PCa diagnosis. These promising findings merit a further investigation.
